concepts.name: Types of Humidity: Absolute, Relative, and Specific Humidity
key_dimensions: Definitions and units of measurement for each type (g/m³ vs g/kg vs percentage)
Why relative humidity is more climatologically significant than absolute humidity
How specific humidity remains constant during adiabatic processes unlike relative humidity
UPSC trap: Relative humidity can change without any addition/removal of water vapor (temperature change alone suffices)

concepts.name: Dew Point Temperature and its Climatological Significance
key_dimensions: Definition: temperature at which air becomes saturated for a given moisture content
Relationship between dew point depression and atmospheric stability/instability
Role of dew point in triggering convective precipitation and thunderstorm forecasting
UPSC trap: Dew point vs frost point distinction; dew point ≠ temperature at which dew forms on surfaces

concepts.name: Saturation Vapour Pressure and its Temperature Dependency
key_dimensions: Clausius-Clapeyron relationship: saturation vapour pressure roughly doubles for every 10°C rise
Why warm air can hold more moisture and implications for tropical vs polar precipitation intensity
Connection to climate change: increased atmospheric moisture in a warmer world amplifies rainfall extremes
UPSC trap: Air does not 'hold' water vapour — saturation is a thermodynamic equilibrium concept, not a physical container

concepts.name: Adiabatic Lapse Rates: Dry Adiabatic (DALR) vs Saturated Adiabatic (SALR)
key_dimensions: DALR ≈ 9.8°C/1000m vs SALR ≈ 4–6°C/1000m and reasons for the difference (latent heat release)
SALR is variable unlike DALR — lower in warm tropical air, higher in cold polar air
Application in determining orographic rainfall distribution (windward vs leeward slopes)
UPSC trap: Föhn/Chinook effect — leeward air is warmer and drier because condensation releases latent heat on windward side

concepts.name: Environmental Lapse Rate (ELR) and Atmospheric Stability
key_dimensions: Three stability states: absolute stability (ELR < SALR), conditional instability (SALR < ELR < DALR), absolute instability (ELR > DALR)
Conditional instability as the most common atmospheric condition and its role in convective storms
Inversion layers as extreme stability zones: types (radiation, subsidence, advection, frontal)
UPSC trap: Stable atmosphere suppresses vertical mixing — linked to smog/pollution trapping episodes over cities like Delhi

concepts.name: Temperature Inversions: Types, Formation, and Effects
key_dimensions: Radiation inversion (surface/ground inversion) — nocturnal cooling, favors frost and fog formation
Subsidence inversion — associated with anticyclones and trade wind belts; suppresses rainfall in deserts
Frontal inversion — warm air overriding cold air at frontal boundaries
UPSC trap: Subsidence inversion explains why subtropical high-pressure belts (Sahara, Atacama) are deserts despite proximity to oceans

concepts.name: Cloud Formation Mechanisms: Lifting Processes
key_dimensions: Four lifting mechanisms: convectional, orographic, frontal (cyclonic), and convergence lifting
Lifting Condensation Level (LCL) — height at which cloud base forms during convective lifting
Why different lifting mechanisms produce different cloud types and precipitation patterns
UPSC trap: Orographic lifting causes rainfall only on windward side; Western Ghats vs Deccan Plateau contrast

concepts.name: Cloud Classification: Luke Howard System and WMO Framework
key_dimensions: Three altitude groups: high clouds (cirro-), middle clouds (alto-), low clouds (strato-/nimbo-) and their height ranges
Vertical development clouds: Cumulus and Cumulonimbus cutting across altitude classifications
Cloud types as weather indicators: cirrus (approaching front), cumulonimbus (thunderstorm/hail), stratus (drizzle)
UPSC trap: Altostratus vs Nimbostratus distinction — only nimbostratus produces significant continuous rainfall despite both being grey sheet clouds

concepts.name: Cumulonimbus Cloud: Structure, Dynamics, and Associated Weather
key_dimensions: Vertical extent from near surface to tropopause (~12–15 km); anvil shape due to tropopause acting as lid
Associated phenomena: lightning, thunder, hail, tornadoes, microbursts, waterspouts
Role in ITCZ and tropical convection; relationship with Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCS)
UPSC trap: Cumulonimbus is the ONLY cloud that produces hail and is associated with aviation hazards (clear air turbulence near anvil)

concepts.name: Fog Types: Radiation, Advection, Upslope, Steam, and Frontal Fog
key_dimensions: Radiation fog — calm, clear nights; valley fog phenomenon; seasonal occurrence over Indo-Gangetic Plain
Advection fog — warm moist air over cold surface; Grand Banks fog (Labrador Current + Gulf Stream), San Francisco Bay fog
UPSC trap: Advection fog can form even in windy conditions unlike radiation fog which requires calm conditions
Steam fog (Arctic sea smoke) — cold air over warm water; opposite thermodynamic process to advection fog

concepts.name: Condensation Nuclei and Aerosols: Role in Cloud Formation
key_dimensions: Types of condensation nuclei: hygroscopic (sea salt, sulfates — most effective), hydrophobic (dust), combustion particles
Clean air vs polluted air cloud microphysics: more nuclei → more but smaller droplets → brighter clouds (Twomey effect)
Indirect aerosol effect on climate: increased cloud albedo and extended cloud lifetime as negative forcing
UPSC trap: Clouds can form even before 100% RH over hygroscopic nuclei; supersaturation is not always required

concepts.name: Precipitation Formation: Bergeron-Findeisen Process vs Collision-Coalescence
key_dimensions: Bergeron process: mixed-phase clouds with ice crystals and supercooled water droplets; vapour pressure difference drives ice crystal growth
Collision-coalescence (warm cloud process): dominant in tropical clouds where temperatures remain above 0°C throughout
Why tropical rainfall is intense despite warm clouds — large maritime condensation nuclei produce fewer but larger droplets
UPSC trap: Most mid-latitude precipitation originates as snow/ice (Bergeron) even if it reaches ground as rain (melting layer concept)

concepts.name: Orographic Rainfall and Rain Shadow Effect
key_dimensions: Mechanism: forced ascent → cooling → condensation → precipitation on windward side
Föhn effect on leeward side: temperature inversion in the valley, desiccating warm-dry winds
Global examples: Western Ghats/Deccan, Rockies/Great Plains, Andes/Atacama, Alps/Po Valley
UPSC trap: Orographic effect amplifies existing moisture-laden winds but does not CREATE precipitation — dry continental winds show no orographic rainfall (e.g., Karakoram in central Asia)

concepts.name: Humidity Measurement Instruments: Hygrometer, Psychrometer, and Radiosonde
key_dimensions: Wet-and-dry bulb psychrometer: principle, wet bulb depression, and its relationship to relative humidity
Hair hygrometer vs capacitance hygrometer: mechanical vs electronic sensing principles
Radiosonde: upper atmosphere humidity profiling and its role in NWP (Numerical Weather Prediction) models
UPSC trap: Wet bulb temperature ≠ dew point temperature; wet bulb is always between dry bulb and dew point temperatures

concepts.name: Global Distribution of Humidity and Cloud Cover Patterns
key_dimensions: ITCZ: highest absolute and relative humidity; persistent cloud cover and convective precipitation
Subtropical high-pressure belts (20–30°N/S): low RH despite proximity to tropical moisture — subsidence inversion role
Polar regions: low absolute humidity (cold air) but high relative humidity; precipitation as snow despite low moisture
UPSC trap: Deserts can have moderate relative humidity at night (radiation cooling) but extremely low absolute humidity — RH alone misleads about aridity

concepts.name: Clouds and Earth's Radiation Budget: Albedo vs Greenhouse Effect
key_dimensions: High thin clouds (cirrus): strong greenhouse warming effect > weak albedo cooling → net warming
Low thick clouds (stratus/stratocumulus): strong albedo cooling > weak greenhouse effect → net cooling
Cloud feedback uncertainty: the single largest source of uncertainty in climate sensitivity estimates (IPCC)
UPSC trap: Not all clouds cool the Earth — cloud radiative effect depends on cloud height, thickness, and optical depth

concepts.name: Evapotranspiration: Potential (PET) vs Actual (AET) and Thornthwaite's Framework
key_dimensions: PET: maximum possible ET under unlimited water supply — function of temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation
AET < PET in water-limited environments; AET = PET in water-surplus environments
Thornthwaite's climate classification based on moisture index (P-PET ratio) — humid, sub-humid, semi-arid, arid
UPSC trap: High temperature regions may have high PET but low AET (deserts) — aridity is defined by P-PET deficit, not temperature alone

concepts.name: Dew, Frost, Mist, and Haze: Distinctions and Formation Conditions
key_dimensions: Dew: liquid water deposition on surfaces cooled below dew point; requires calm, clear, humid nights
Frost: direct deposition of ice when surface temperature drops below frost point (<0°C); white frost vs black frost distinction
Mist vs Fog: visibility distinction (fog < 1 km; mist 1–2 km) and density; same formation mechanism
UPSC trap: Haze ≠ fog/mist — haze is dry (dust/smoke particles), reduces visibility without water condensation; significant in Delhi winter air quality

concepts.name: Urban Heat Island Effect on Local Humidity and Cloud Formation
key_dimensions: Reduced evapotranspiration in cities → lower absolute humidity despite higher temperatures → lower RH
Urban-induced convection: enhanced sensible heat flux triggers afternoon convective clouds and precipitation downwind of cities
Urban aerosol loading: more CCN → modified cloud microphysics, altered precipitation patterns

UPSC trap: Cities are often drier (lower absolute humidity) than surrounding rural areas due to impervious surfaces despite producing more heat — counterintuitive but important for smart city planning
